title: Improving Dynamical Decoupling for Trapped-Ion QCCD Quantum Computers
authors: William M. Watkins, Leigh M. Norris, Ross Hutson, Maxwell Urmey, Peter Siegfried, Charles H. Baldwin
abstract: We examine the impact of scheduling errors on dynamical decoupling (DD) in trapped-ion quantum charge-coupled devices (QCCDs) and develop better strategies for reducing memory errors. In the QCCD architecture, qubit transport and control introduce stochastic pulse delays that impact the efficiency of DD. Using the filter-function formalism, we analyze the performance of DD in the presence of scheduling-induced timing errors, showing that they increase the sensitivity of standard DD to low-frequency fluctuations. For typical memory errors in trapped-ion platforms, we numerically demonstrate that increasing the DD pulse frequency beyond 2 Hz is generally counterproductive due to scheduling-induced timing errors. Furthermore, we introduce a real-time DD protocol that inserts refocusing pulses opportunistically during idle periods. We demonstrate our methods on Quantinuum H2-1 with Ramsey delay-type experiments.
summary: This paper investigates the impact of timing inaccuracies, or scheduling errors, on Dynamical Decoupling sequences used to protect qubits in trapped-ion QCCD quantum computers. Using advanced noise filtering techniques, the authors show that these real-world hardware imperfections limit the effectiveness of standard error suppression protocols. They introduce a novel, adaptive DD protocol that dynamically adjusts refocusing pulses during idle times to maintain high fidelity.
main_problem: The paper addresses how scheduling errors, inherent in trapped-ion QCCD architectures, degrade the performance of Dynamical Decoupling (DD) sequences designed to suppress memory errors.
main_result: Scheduling errors increase DD sensitivity to low-frequency noise, making high pulse frequencies counterproductive; a real-time protocol that opportunistically refocuses pulses is proposed as an improvement.
method: The analysis employs the Filter Function formalism and cumulant expansion techniques to model noise suppression in the presence of stochastic timing deviations from ideal gate sequences.
model_or_system: The system is trapped-ion QCCD quantum computers, modeled using an effective qubit Hamiltonian subject to low-frequency magnetic field fluctuations ($\propto \sigma_z$). The analysis extends DD theory from deterministic control to stochastic control incorporating pulse timing jitter.
key_observables: Survival probability ($P$), the second cumulant $C^{(2)}(T)$, and the Control Filter Function $F(\omega, T)$.
important_parameters: The critical threshold for DD pulse frequency (around 2 Hz) where scheduling errors become dominant; the spectral dependence of noise ($S(2\pi f)$).
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include treating $\pi$-pulses as instantaneous and assuming that scheduling errors are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.).
figures_summary: Figures show filter functions for CPMG sequences, empirical distributions of timing offsets ($\epsilon$), and survival probabilities demonstrating the plateauing fidelity improvement due to accumulated scheduling error.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing standard DD theory using the Filter Function formalism to incorporating stochastic scheduling errors via cumulant expansions. It culminates in proposing and analyzing a real-time, opportunistic refocusing protocol for improved robustness.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges fundamental quantum control theory (DD) with practical hardware limitations (scheduling jitter), providing actionable insights for building fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum processors.

The pulses are injected at compile time and placed as close to T/2 as possible, where T is the idle time between single-qubit gates on a given qubit. A CPMG or PDD sequence with N = 1 prescribes that the pulse takes place at T/2, but because of a limited number of gate zones, the pulse is applied either earlier or later than desired.
